problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(k-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=4\,m/s$ at the origin and the particle has velocity $v=2\sqrt{6}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $2\,m,$ find the value of $k.$

activity_context.topic_title: Determining Properties of Objects Described as Functions of Displacement

examples.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,\rm{m},$ the velocity is $v\,\rm{m/s},$ and the acceleration is $2kx\,\rm{m/s}^2,$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ at the origin and the particle has velocity $v=4\,\rm{m/s}$ when its displacement is $1 \,\rm{m},$ find the value of $k.$
examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094268/assets/6280c4b1561cda0d16c6758bb5d8fae30d66d9925bd1bb9db1a29e70093c6f61.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $2kx\,\rm{m/s}^2,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} =2 kx.
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = 2kx.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) \textrm{d}x = \int 2kx \:\textrm{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\dfrac12v^2 = kx^2 + C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ when $x=0\,\rm{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =k(0)^{2}+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\dfrac12v^2 = kx^2 + 2.
$$

Finally, since $v=4\,\rm{m/s}$ when $x=1\,\rm{m},$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k{x}^{2}+2 \\ \frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & =k(1)^{2}+2 \\ 8 & =k+2 \\ k & =6\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x\ge \frac{1}{2}.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s,$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $(4x-2)\,{m/s}^{2},$ and the acceleration is directed toward $O.$
If $P$ has velocity $1\,m/s$ when its displacement is $\frac{1}{2}\,m,$ find the value of $x$ for which $P$ is instantaneously at rest.
feedback.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094268/assets/cdb88c0c679ca9325df42c5c8c4feaea6ce6c0cf02655410158860d7b03d54dc.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $(4x-2)\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-(4x-2).
$$

Using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-(4x-2).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (-4x+2)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2{x}^{2}+2x+C.
$$

Now, since $v=1\,m/s$ when $x=\frac{1}{2}\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-2{x}^{2}+2x+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(1)^{2} & =-2{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+2(\frac{1}{2})+C \\ C & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}-1 \\ C & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=-2{x}^{2}+2x.
$$

Finally, the particle is instantaneously at rest when $v(x)=0\,m/s.$ We find the displacement of the particle when instantaneously at rest by substituting $v=0$ in the equation above and solving for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =-2{x}^{2}+2x \\ \frac{1}{2}(0)^{2} & =-2{x}^{2}+2x \\ 2x(1-x) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The only solution of this equation for $x\ge \frac{1}{2}$ is $x=1\,m.$
